requests.prompt_text: The lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs every evening at dusk, counting the one hundred and twelve steps out of habit rather than need. From the gallery he could see the fishing boats returning along the channel, their lamps swinging as the swell lifted them. He had kept the light for thirty years, through storms that tore slates from the village roofs and through long calm summers when the sea lay flat as a sheet of tin. The lamp itself had changed twice in that time, first from oil to acetylene and then to electricity, but the rhythm of the work had not changed at all: trim, clean, wind, watch. His daughter wrote from the city that the service would automate the station within the decade, and he supposed she was right, though he did not see how a machine would know to listen for the foghorn of the coastal steamer and answer it twice. On clear nights he read the almanac by the light of the lamp room and marked the tides in pencil in the margin. The keeper's log recorded the weather, the visibility, the passing ships and, once a year, the arrival of the inspector, who always remarked on the polish of the brass and never on the view. What makes the method fragile in practice is not the arithmetic but the invariants at the boundaries, where an off-by-one error turns a correct loop into one that never terminates or that skips the very element it was asked to find. Careful implementations therefore state the invariant explicitly, for example that the answer always lies in the half-open interval, and they prove that each iteration preserves it while shrinking the interval by at least one element.
